summary: Specifies how a Binary Floor Control Protocol client connects to a floor control server outside of an offer/answer exchange. Authentication of client and server uses TLS. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: A floor control server decides who may speak in a conference. A client normally learns where the server is from the session description that set the call up. This document covers the other case: a client that has to connect on its own, with no session description to lean on. It says how to open the connection, how to prove who each side is, and how to reconnect afterwards.

questions: how does a bfcp client connect to a server
how does a bfcp client connect to a floor control server
subtitle: How a BFCP client connects to a floor control server when there is no SDP offer/answer to lean on, and how each side proves who it is.

tldr.problem: A client of the Binary Floor Control Protocol (BFCP) needs to open a connection to a floor control server, but outside an SDP offer/answer exchange there is no protected channel for swapping certificate fingerprints.
tldr.mechanism: The client opens a TCP connection and runs TLS over it. The server always acts as the TLS server and proves its identity with a certificate, while the client proves itself with a pre-shared secret using PSK-TLS.
tldr.outcome: BFCP connections made outside offer/answer get a defined way to connect, reconnect and authenticate both ends. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and was later updated by RFC 8996.

today: RFC 5018 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2007. It has not been obsoleted, but it was updated by RFC 8996.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
As discussed in the BFCP specification, a given BFCP client needs a set of data in order to establish a BFCP connection to a floor control server. These data include the transport address of the server, the conference identifier, and the user identifier. It is outside the scope of this document to specify how a client obtains this information, and the document assumes that the client obtains it using an out-of-band method.

Once the client obtains this information, it needs to establish a BFCP connection to the floor control server, and the way this connection is established depends on the context of the client and the server. How to establish such a connection in the context of an SDP offer/answer exchange between a client and a floor control server is specified in RFC 4583. This document specifies how a client establishes a connection to a floor control server outside the context of an SDP offer/answer exchange.

BFCP entities establishing a connection outside an SDP offer/answer exchange need different authentication mechanisms than entities using offer/answer exchanges. This is because offer/answer exchanges provide the parties with an initial integrity-protected channel that clients and floor control servers can use to exchange the fingerprints of their self-signed certificates. Outside the offer/answer model, such a channel is not typically available. This document specifies how to authenticate clients using PSK-TLS and how to authenticate servers using server certificates.
sections.plainLanguage: A floor control server decides who may speak in a conference. A client normally learns where the server is from the session description that set the call up. This document covers the other case: a client that has to connect on its own, with no session description to lean on. It says how to open the connection, how to prove who each side is, and how to reconnect afterwards.

sections.title: TCP Connection Establishment
sections.content:
Once the client has the transport address, that is the IP address and port, of the floor control server, it initiates a TCP connection towards it. That is, the client performs an active TCP open.

If the client is provided with the floor control server's host name instead of with its IP address, the client MUST perform a DNS lookup in order to resolve the host name into an IP address. Clients eventually perform an A or AAAA DNS lookup, or both, on the host name. In order to translate the target to the corresponding set of IP addresses, IPv6-only or dual-stack clients MUST use name resolution functions that implement the Source and Destination Address Selection algorithms specified in RFC 3484. On many hosts that support IPv6, APIs like getaddrinfo() provide this functionality and subsume existing APIs like gethostbyname().

The advantage of the additional complexity is that this technique outputs an ordered list of IPv6 and IPv4 destination addresses based on the relative merits of the corresponding source and destination pairs, which results in the selection of a preferred destination address. The RFC notes that these algorithms depend on broad operating system support and uniform implementation of the application programming interfaces, and points developers to the issues described by Roy et al. with respect to address resolution delays and address selection rules. For example, implementations of getaddrinfo() may return address lists containing IPv6 global addresses at the top of the list and IPv4 addresses at the bottom, even when the host is only configured with an IPv6 local scope and an IPv4 address, which introduces a delay in completing the connection.

The BFCP specification describes a number of situations when the TCP connection between a client and the floor control server needs to be reestablished, but does not describe the reestablishment process, because that process depends on how the connection was established in the first place. When the existing TCP connection is closed following the rules in the BFCP specification, the client SHOULD reestablish the connection towards the floor control server. If a TCP connection cannot deliver a BFCP message from the client to the floor control server and times out, the client SHOULD reestablish the TCP connection.
sections.plainLanguage: The client opens the connection to the server itself, without waiting to be called. If it only has the server's name it looks it up in the DNS, and on a machine with both IPv4 and IPv6 it uses the standard address selection rules to pick the best address. If the connection drops or a message times out, the client opens a new one the same way.

sections.title: TLS Usage
sections.content:
The BFCP specification requires that all BFCP entities implement TLS and recommends that they use it in all their connections. TLS provides integrity and replay protection, and optional confidentiality. The floor control server MUST always act as the TLS server, so the client is always the one that starts the handshake.

A floor control server that receives a BFCP message over plain TCP, with no TLS, SHOULD request the use of TLS by generating an Error message with an Error code with a value of 9, Use TLS.
sections.plainLanguage: Everything runs inside TLS. The server is always the one that plays the server role in the TLS handshake, and the client plays the client role. A client that sends a message in the clear gets an error back telling it to use TLS.

sections.title: Certificate-Based Server Authentication
sections.content:
At TLS connection establishment the floor control server MUST present its certificate to the client. The certificate provided at the TLS level MUST either be directly signed by one of the other party's trust anchors, or be validated using a certification path that terminates at one of the other party's trust anchors.

A client establishing a connection to a server knows the server's host name or IP address. If the client knows the server's host name, the client MUST check it against the server's identity as presented in the server's Certificate message, in order to prevent man-in-the-middle attacks. If a subjectAltName extension of type dNSName is present, that MUST be used as the identity. Otherwise, the most specific Common Name field in the Subject field of the certificate MUST be used. Although the use of the Common Name is existing practice, it is deprecated, and Certification Authorities are encouraged to use the subjectAltName instead.

Matching is performed using the matching rules of the certificate profile. If more than one identity of a given type is present in the certificate, a match in any one of the set is considered acceptable. Names in Common Name fields may contain the wildcard character, which is considered to match any single domain name component or component fragment: *.a.com matches foo.a.com but not bar.foo.a.com, and f*.com matches foo.com but not bar.com.

If the client does not know the server's host name and contacts the server directly using the server's IP address, the iPAddress subjectAltName must be present in the certificate and must exactly match the IP address known to the client. If the host name or IP address known to the client does not match the identity in the certificate, user-oriented clients MUST either notify the user, and may give the user the opportunity to continue with the connection in any case, or terminate the connection with a bad certificate error. Automated clients MUST log the error to an appropriate audit log, if one is available, and SHOULD terminate the connection with a bad certificate error. Automated clients MAY provide a configuration setting that disables this check, but MUST provide a setting that enables it.
sections.plainLanguage: The server proves who it is with a certificate. The client checks the certificate against the name or address it was trying to reach, so that a fake server in the middle cannot pass. A mismatch is fatal for an automated client, and for a person at a terminal it must at least be shown.

sections.title: Client Authentication Based on a Pre-Shared Secret
sections.content:
Client authentication is based on a pre-shared secret between client and server, and authentication is performed using PSK-TLS.

The BFCP specification mandates support for the TLS_RSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA ciphersuite. Additionally, clients and servers supporting this specification MUST support the TLS_RSA_PSK_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA ciphersuite as well.
sections.plainLanguage: The client proves who it is with a secret that both sides already share. The ciphersuite TLS_RSA_PSK_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA must be supported by every client and server that implements this document.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Client and server authentication as specified in this document are based on the use of TLS, so it is strongly RECOMMENDED that TLS with non-null encryption is always used. Clients and floor control servers MAY use other security mechanisms as long as they provide similar security properties, namely replay and integrity protection, confidentiality, and client and server authentication.

TLS PSK simply relies on a pre-shared key without specifying the nature of the key. In practice such keys have two sources: text passwords and randomly generated binary keys. When keys are derived from passwords, TLS PSK mode is subject to offline dictionary attacks. In DHE and RSA modes, an attacker who can mount a single man-in-the-middle attack on a client and server pair can then mount a dictionary attack on the password. In modes without DHE or RSA, an attacker who can record communications between a client and server pair can mount a dictionary attack on the password. It is therefore RECOMMENDED that, where possible, clients use certificate-based server authentication ciphersuites with password-derived PSKs, in order to defend against dictionary attacks.

Passwords SHOULD be chosen with enough entropy to provide some protection against dictionary attacks. Because the entropy of text varies dramatically and is generally far less than that of an equivalent random bitstring, no hard and fast rules about password length are possible, but in general passwords SHOULD be at least 8 characters and selected from a pool containing both upper and lower case, numbers and special keyboard characters. An 8-character ASCII password has a maximum entropy of 56 bits and in general far lower. If possible, passphrases are preferable to passwords, and it is RECOMMENDED that implementations support, at minimum, 16-character passwords or passphrases. A cooperating client and server pair MAY choose to derive the TLS PSK shared key from the passphrase via a password-based key derivation function such as PBKDF2, which may incorporate iteration functions for key strengthening and so provides some additional protection against dictionary attacks by increasing the amount of work the attacker must perform.

When the keys are randomly generated and of sufficient length, dictionary attacks are not effective, because such keys are highly unlikely to be in the attacker's dictionary. Where possible, keys SHOULD be generated using a strong random number generator, and a minimum key length of 80 bits SHOULD be used.

The remainder of the section analyses the threats against BFCP and how they are addressed. An attacker may attempt to impersonate a client, a floor participant or a floor chair, in order to generate forged floor requests or to grant or deny existing floor requests; client impersonation is avoided by using TLS, and the floor control server assumes that attackers cannot hijack TLS connections from authenticated clients. An attacker may attempt to impersonate a floor control server, which would let clients believe they hold a particular floor and so try to access a resource they have no right to; server impersonation is avoided by having floor control servers present their server certificates at TLS connection establishment time. Attackers may attempt to modify messages exchanged by a client and a floor control server, which the integrity protection provided by TLS connections prevents. Attackers may attempt to pick messages from the network to get access to confidential information between the floor control server and a client, such as why a floor request was denied, which TLS confidentiality prevents; for that reason it is RECOMMENDED that TLS is used with a non-null encryption algorithm.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC insists on encryption, and it is careful about the one weak spot of a shared secret: a short password can be guessed offline. It recommends long passwords or passphrases, or a random key of at least 80 bits, and a key derivation function that makes each guess slower. TLS itself is what stops impersonation, tampering and eavesdropping.

viz.caption: HOW EACH SIDE PROVES WHO IT IS

cells: Presents a certificate when the TLS connection is established
The certificate matches the host name or IP address it wanted to reach
Uses PSK-TLS with a pre-shared secret
The secret it already shares with the server

viz.caption: THE THREATS AND WHAT STOPS THEM

items.title: Client impersonation
items.text: Stopped by TLS; the server assumes the channel cannot be hijacked.

items.title: Server impersonation
items.text: Stopped by the server presenting its certificate.

items.title: Message modification
items.text: Stopped by the integrity protection in TLS.

items.title: Eavesdropping
items.text: Stopped by TLS confidentiality, so use a non-null cipher.

items.title: Password guessing
items.text: Use a long passphrase, or a random key of at least 80 bits.
